verdict.rationale: Christian nationalism is a modern political category with no Greek or Hebrew lexeme (a basic dictionary word form) that names it, so the proposition cannot be settled by direct word study. The supplied anchors lean against fusing nation and kingdom: John 18:36 sources the kingdom as 'out of this world' (ek tou kosmou toutou) where 'from, out of' (ek) with the 'from-X' grammatical form (the genitive) marks origin rather than mere location, Philippians 3:20 places 'commonwealth or citizenship' (to politeuma) 'in the heavens' (en ouranois) though 'commonwealth or citizenship' (politeuma) itself is a single New Testament occurrence so its precise civic scope cannot be triangulated, Galatians 3:28 relativizes 'Jew' (Ioudaios) and 'Greek' (Hellen) in the one Christ identity, and Revelation 5:9-10 constitutes the redeemed people as drawn 'out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation' (ek pases phyles kai glosses kai laou kai ethnous). Against this stand Romans 13:1 with 'be subject to' (hypotasso), 'authority' (exousia), and 'having been ordained' (tetagmenai) marking civil order as divinely ordained, and the Old Testament national-covenant pattern not in the Greek bundle. The canon supplies two patterns the words do not rank, so the precise boundary the proposition draws stays a contested lexical inference.

scripture.force: Jesus says 'my kingdom is not of this world' (he basileia he eme ouk estin ek tou kosmou toutou). The preposition 'from, out of' (ek) with a noun in the 'from-X' grammatical form (the genitive) marks origin and source, not mere location, so the claim is that the kingdom does not derive its power or legitimacy from worldly polity (the political order or government). The contrary-to-fact 'if-then' clause (conditional) that follows, 'if my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting' (ei ek tou kosmou toutou en he basileia he eme, hoi hyperetai hoi emoi egonizonto), ties the point to the refusal of armed national struggle. This cuts against treating any nation state as the vehicle of Christ's reign.

'For our commonwealth or citizenship is in the heavens' (hemon gar to politeuma en ouranois hyparchei). The noun 'commonwealth or citizenship' (politeuma) occurs exactly once in the New Testament, a hapax legomenon (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), which means its precise civic scope cannot be triangulated from canon usage and must be inferred from word formation (the politeu stem of 'commonwealth or polity') and from this single context. It is placed 'in the heavens' (en ouranois) with 'exists, subsists' (hyparchei) stressing settled existence, and a Savior is awaited 'from which' (ex hou). The locative phrase relativizes earthly national citizenship as the locus of ultimate allegiance, but the hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) leaves open whether earthly citizenship is replaced, subordinated, or simply de-centered.

'There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus' (ouk eni Ioudaios oude Hellen, ouk eni doulos oude eleutheros, ouk eni arsen kai thely, pantes gar hymeis heis este en Christo Iesou). The ethnic pair 'Jew' (Ioudaios) and 'Greek' (Hellen) is the first abolished boundary, and 'you are one' (heis este) declares one corporate identity in Christ. The verb 'there is' (eni, contracted enesti, 'there is') negates the in-Christ standing of these distinctions, not their continued empirical existence, so national markers are demoted as grounds of standing without being erased as social categories.

The new song praises the Lamb who 'purchased for God by your blood out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation' (egorasas to theo en to haimati sou ek pases phyles kai glosses kai laou kai ethnous). The fourfold 'out of' (ek) phrase, with 'from, out of' (ek) again marking source, makes the redeemed a body purchased out of all nations rather than coextensive with any one 'nation' (ethnos). The piling up of 'tribe' (phyle), 'tongue' (glossa), 'people' (laos), and 'nation' (ethnos) covers tribal, linguistic, ethnic, and political categories together, so no one nation can be the bearer of the kingdom.

'And you made them to our God a kingdom and priests, and they will reign upon the earth' (kai epoiesas autous to theo hemon basileian kai hiereis, kai basileusousin epi tes ges). The redeemed from all nations are themselves made a 'kingdom' (basileia), a kingdom and priests, who will 'reign' (basileusousin, future of basileuo) upon the earth. The kingdom is constituted of the cross-national redeemed and reigns by divine action expressed in 'you made' (epoiesas, an aorist [a completed past action] of accomplished constitution), not as the political ascendancy of a particular nation state.

complicating_texts.resolution: Direct lexical query confirms Romans 13:1 contains 'be subject to' (hupotasso, G5293, 40 New Testament occurrences) governing 'every soul' (pasa psyche), with 'governing authorities' (exousiais hyperechousais) and the verbal 'having been ordained' (tetagmenai, from G5021 'tasso', meaning ordered) governed by 'by God' (hypo theou). The grammar makes civil authority the object of divine ordering, which is not the same as making any specific nation state the vehicle of Christ's kingdom but is also not its abolition. The text grounds a separate sphere of obedience to civil order that the proposition's caution should not flatten, leaving the precise boundary contested by the canon, not by the words alone.

Israel is called 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (mamleket kohanim ve goy qadosh), where 'nation' (goy) denotes the political-ethnic nation. The lexical store loaded for this query is Greek only (no Hebrew tokens returned for H1471 'nation' (goy) or H5971 'people' (am)), so the Old Testament national-covenant pattern cannot be word-studied here. The Revelation 5:10 echo, 'a kingdom and priests' (basileia kai hiereis), lexically transfers the formula to the cross-national redeemed, but whether this transfer exhausts or coexists with a holy-nation pattern is not resolvable from the available bundle.

Lexical query confirms 'resident alien' (paroikos, G3941, 4 New Testament occurrences) and 'sojourning stranger' (parepidemos, G3927, 3 New Testament occurrences) co-occur here as 'resident aliens and sojourning strangers' (paroikous kai parepidemous), technical terms for resident alien and sojourning stranger. Their rarity (combined seven occurrences) means the in-the-world but not-of-it stance is articulated by a small but precise vocabulary, consistent with the Philippians 3:20 'commonwealth or citizenship' (politeuma) cluster but not lexically prescriptive about specific civic structures.

The Revelation 5:10 reading 'kingdom' (basileian) and 'they will reign' (basileusousin) carries minor textual fluctuation but does not alter the multinational, divinely constituted kingdom sense, so the verdict is variant robust.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading John 18:36 'out of this world' (ek tou kosmou toutou) and Philippians 3:20 'commonwealth or citizenship in the heavens' (politeuma en ouranois) as marking a distinct heavenly polity (political community) supports caution toward fusing the nation state with Christ's kingdom, since the church's citizenship and the civil order are kept on separate planes and the kingdom is sourced from outside the world.

If the Exodus 19:6 pattern of 'holy nation' (goy qadosh) and the Romans 13:1 ordination of 'authorities' (exousiai) by God carry into the new covenant era as a continuing template for civil order under Christ's lordship, then a nation that orders its laws toward Christ is not lexically excluded, leaving the proposition contested rather than settled by the cited anchors.

Tracing the covenant arc from one national people to a multinational body purchased 'out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation' (ek pases phyles kai glosses kai laou kai ethnous) in Revelation 5:9 demotes any single nation as the vehicle of the kingdom and reads 'a kingdom and priests' (basileia kai hiereis) of Revelation 5:10 as the eschatological (end-time) fulfillment of Exodus 19:6, transferring the holy-nation pattern to the redeemed of all nations.

If Christ's lordship in Revelation 5:10 extends 'upon the earth' (epi tes ges, over the earth) and Romans 13 marks civil authority as ordained by God, a transformationalist lens reads this as a mandate to bring national life under Christ's reign through Christian witness, which the cited words neither prescribe nor forbid since they speak of the source and constitution of the kingdom rather than its mode of civic engagement.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether the new covenant arc transforms the Old Testament national-covenant pattern into a cross-national people, and on how the heavenly 'commonwealth or citizenship' (politeuma) relates to ongoing earthly civic responsibility. The cited Greek anchors lean toward the former, but the bundle omits Hebrew theocratic texts and the precise vocabulary cluster of Romans 13, so the lens conflict cannot be fully adjudicated lexically and each framework above is given in its strongest form.

lay_summary: The phrase Christian nationalism is a modern political idea, and no single Greek or Hebrew word in the Bible names it, so we cannot settle this question by looking up one term. We have to read the verses the question points to and let the words do the work. In John 18:36 Jesus tells Pilate that his kingdom is not 'out of this world' (ek tou kosmou toutou). The small word 'from, out of' (ek) with what follows it points to where something comes from, like saying water out of a spring, so Jesus is saying the source of his reign is not worldly government, and he refuses to let his followers fight for it by force. In Philippians 3:20 Paul says our 'commonwealth or citizenship' (politeuma) is in the heavens. Here is one important lexical limit. The word 'commonwealth or citizenship' (politeuma) appears only once in the whole New Testament (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), so we cannot triangulate its exact scope by comparing other uses. It clearly puts a believer's deepest belonging above any earthly nation, but it does not by itself spell out how Christians should engage civic life. In Galatians 3:28 the labels 'Jew' (Ioudaios) and 'Greek' (Hellen) are set aside because all are 'one' (heis) in Christ, which lowers the importance of ethnic and national identity as a basis for standing before God. In Revelation 5:9-10 the Lamb purchases people 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation' (ek pases phyles kai glosses kai laou kai ethnous), and those redeemed people, drawn from all nations, are themselves made a 'kingdom' (basileia) and priests. The piling up of four categories together rules out coextending the kingdom with any one nation. Pulling the other way is Romans 13:1, where the words 'be subject to' (hypotasso), 'authority' (exousia), and 'ordained' (tetagmenai) make civil order something God himself sets up. The Bible therefore gives us two patterns: a kingdom sourced from outside the world and centered in the redeemed of all nations, and civil authority ordained by God. The words do not rank these two patterns, and the question's specific phrase 'to be regarded with caution and largely rejected' goes further than the vocabulary by itself requires. That is why the lexical evidence here is best described as contested rather than decisive.
